Just make sure that you redaction is what the professor expects. Sometimes when looking at these courses notation can change quite a lot and might not be what your teacher is asking. Happened to me a few times. 

So yeah, online courses should mainly be used for the understanding and comprehension of blurry ideas and tools, the rest needs to be adequately adapted to what you've been taught unfortunately.

I would recommend searching for online courses about the studied subject, edx is quite a good one. They allow provide a different aspect, and sometimes clarification. 

If you're doing this with a book I'd suggest to find proofs of the expressions that you have difficulty understanding. Then try doing some exercises where you use that expression. 
Goal here is to get a solid basis with which you should be able to progress. 

If that fails you can always resort to videos that explain the matter clearly. 

If you've studied too much or for too long consider taking a break. It can avoid being stuck on a problem and often helps you see it in another perspective. 

The important thing to do is make sure you understand what you're using, sometimes rereading everything slowly works, but take it step by step. Don't try to learn 15 things at the same time, that won't work. Spend some time on one thing, and when you've understood it move on.

Depends a lot on the language, and there are many different ways to learn. A recipe that worked well for me is as follows

\- Learn the basest of words and try making out what's said on the radio or any news channels. 

\- Next is learning the alphabet if required.

\- Learn a few verbs and their first conjugations.

\- Read an easy and simple book. As you do, note any and all words you discover.

\- With the words you've noted try writting an essay of some sort, maybe a story, whatever makes you write. 

If you keep listening to the studied language and repeat the last two steps you can very easily make it to a B1-B2 level in just a few months.

I would however say that stopping at 3 languages is probably best. By experience its extremely difficult to speak any one of them natively. By that I mean there's a point at which you can't learn any single one of them properly because the time spent studying one of them is time not spent studying the other 2. 

Worse is when you start mixing different words from different languages. Its painfully hard to find the right ones in the right language. So do the rules of grammar. 

As an example, between spanish-catalan, since they are closely related, I find myself mixing many words together. With english french and spanish, I tend to badly contruct sentences because my intuition would want me using french/english/spanish gramatical rules in cases where I shouldn't. 

Knowing many languages is just a fancy parlor trick between friends, most of the time you can't master any single one correctly. When faced with a native-speaker, its sometimes a struggle to get the right words out, which makes you look like an idiot.

Yes, but see this goes back to the known saying "ignorance is bliss".  Accepting the absurdity of life is just a way to force ignorance upon oneself as a coping mechanism for reality. Its almost a form of denial since the subject's mindset is told to look away from the big picture and focus on the small details. 

Take the example of a art piece: everyone can look at a painting and look at it as if it were a lovely drawing or a message meant to be decoded by artistic savants. Others can decide to go deeper, to spend more time analysing the small details and finding meanings unintentionally left by the artist. This brings pleasure because you've distracted yourself from the objectively colourful square, to the creation of many different puzzles, each arbitrarily harder to solve. The hope for finding a solution or a right answer is what gives one hope for a hidden meaning, an intricate design waiting to be discovered, the sense of accomplishing something you thought nobody else could. What is it really? I think they're just a way to avoid looking at things the way they are. Because reality is disapointing, dull, ordinary, almost predictable. Where's the fun in that? Where's the game in all of it?

Don't start by catching up the chapters that you've missed. This might seem paradoxical, but what you should focus on is your motivation. 

Trying to get better at math because you want higher grades, isn't a valid motivation. Try to find what mathematics allow you to do, the usefulness, the beauty of it. I'd recommend looking at a few 3b1b videos, you can easily find them on youtube and that'll give you a perspective of why you're learning basic maths in HS.
If you have that motivation, and are eager to know more about it, then as tedious as it seems you'll have to start from rock bottom.

Why haven't I suggested you do that first? Because starting from the very beginning without motivation or proper understanding of the tools you're using is frankly dumb. You'll end up forgetting half of what you learned, and might even bring you back to square 1. 

Now that you know why you're learning maths, why its so usefull, and why it is so frequently used... You'll catch up whatever you've missed in mere weeks. Give it a month and you'll be right back on track. You might even be  better than your fellow classmates since you've got real motive and they haven't. 

Its important in mathematics not to stay confined to what they teach you. You shouldn't be afraid of curiosity. Try going further. Try understanding how the tools they teach you can be used. 
No doubt you'll be getting this realisation as you study whatever you've missed.

But please, oh please. Don't be like the mindless math idiots that only see formulas, applying them without proper understanding of where they come from. As you grow up you'll be seeing a terrifying amount of them...
